name: Mirtazapine
className: Antidepressant (presynaptic alpha-2 antagonist; noradrenergic and serotonergic)

formulations.label: Film-coated tablets
formulations.note: Scored; can be divided into equal doses. Contains lactose.

src.q: Each Mirtazapine 30 mg film-coated tablet contains 30 mg of mirtazapine.
The tablet can be divided into equal doses.
Each Mirtazapine 30 mg film-coated tablet contains 225.750 mg lactose monohydrate.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Adults: episodes of major depression.

src.q: Mirtazapine is indicated in adults for the treatment of episodes of major depression.

items.t: Not for children and adolescents under 18 (efficacy not shown; safety concerns).

src.q: Mirtazapine should not be used in children and adolescents under the age of 18 years as efficacy was not demonstrated in two short-term clinical trials

items.t: Start 15 mg or 30 mg daily; usual effective dose 15 mg to 45 mg daily. Effect usually after 1 to 2 weeks; response expected within 2 to 4 weeks. If response is poor, increase up to the maximum; if still no response after a further 2 to 4 weeks, stop. Treat at least 6 months.

src.q: The effective daily dose is usually between 15 and 45 mg; the starting dose is 15 or 30 mg.
Treatment with an adequate dose should result in a positive response within 2-4 weeks.
If there is no response within a further 2-4 weeks, then treatment should be stopped.
Patients with depression should be treated for a sufficient period of at least 6 months to ensure that they are free from symptoms.

items.t: Elderly: same dose as adults; increase only under close supervision.

src.q: In elderly patients an increase in dosing should be done under close supervision to elicit a satisfactory and safe response.

items.t: Stopping: discontinue gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms.

src.q: It is recommended to discontinue treatment with mirtazapine gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms

items.t: With carbamazepine or other enzyme inducers the dose may need increasing (and reducing when the inducer is stopped). With potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, azole antifungals, erythromycin, HIV protease inhibitors or cimetidine the dose may need reducing.

src.q: When carbamazepine or any other inducer of hepatic metabolism (such as rifampicin) is added to mirtazapine therapy, the mirtazapine dose may have to be increased.

Caution should be exercised and the dose may have to be decreased when co-administering mirtazapine with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, HIV protease inhibitors, azole antifungals, erythromycin, cimetidine or nefazodone.

items.t: Should not be used under 18 years. Paediatric trials did not show efficacy; suicidal behaviour and hostility were more frequent with antidepressants; marked weight gain, urticaria and raised triglycerides seen.

src.q: Mirtazapine should not be used in the treatment of children and adolescents under the age of 18 years.
The following adverse events were observed commonly in clinical trials in children: weight gain, urticaria and hypertriglyceridaemia

items.t: Hypersensitivity to mirtazapine or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1 .

items.t: Use with MAO inhibitors (and within 2 weeks of stopping one; about 2 weeks should pass after mirtazapine before starting one).

src.q: Concomitant use of mirtazapine with monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors
Mirtazapine should not be administered concomitantly with MAO inhibitors or within two weeks after discontinuation of MAO inhibitor therapy.

items.t: Bone marrow depression (granulocytopenia, agranulocytosis), occasionally fatal, mostly over 65 years: stop and check blood count if fever, sore throat, stomatitis or other signs of infection.

src.q: Bone marrow depression, usually presenting as granulocytopenia or agranulocytosis, has been reported during treatment with Mirtazapine.
when such symptoms occur, treatment should be stopped and blood counts taken

items.t: Careful dosing and regular close monitoring needed in: epilepsy or organic brain syndrome, hepatic or renal impairment, cardiac disease (conduction disturbance, angina, recent MI), low blood pressure, diabetes (close monitoring; antidiabetic dose may need adjustment).

src.q: Careful dosing as well as regular and close monitoring is necessary in patients with:
cardiac diseases like conduction disturbances, angina pectoris and recent myocardial infarction, where normal precautions should be taken and concomitant medicines carefully administered
Insulin and/or oral hypoglycaemic dosage may need to be adjusted and close monitoring is recommended.

items.t: Epilepsy: introduce cautiously; stop if seizures develop or become more frequent.

src.q: Mirtazapine should be introduced cautiously in patients who have a history of seizures.
Treatment should be discontinued in any patient who develops seizures, or where there is an increase in seizure frequency.

items.t: QT prolongation, torsade de pointes and sudden death reported post-marketing (mostly overdose or other risk factors): caution with cardiovascular disease, family history of QT prolongation or other QT-prolonging drugs.

src.q: Cases of QT prolongation, Torsades de Pointes, ventricular tachycardia, and sudden death, have been reported during the post-marketing use of mirtazapine.
Caution should be exercised when Mirtazapine is prescribed in patients with known cardiovascular disease or family history of QT prolongation

items.t: Schizophrenia/psychosis: symptoms may worsen. Bipolar: may switch to mania; monitor closely, stop if manic. Prostate hypertrophy, micturition problems, narrow-angle glaucoma or raised eye pressure: take care.

src.q: Worsening of psychotic symptoms can occur when antidepressants are administered to patients with schizophrenia or other psychotic disturbances
Patients with a history of mania/hypomania should be closely monitored. Mirtazapine should be discontinued in any patient entering a manic phase.
Care should be taken in patients with micturition disturbances like prostate hypertrophy and in patients with acute narrow-angle glaucoma and increased intra-ocular pressure

items.t: Suicidal thoughts/behaviour: close supervision early and after dose changes; give the smallest quantity consistent with good care (overdose risk).

src.q: Close supervision of patients and in particular those at high risk should accompany therapy with antidepressants especially in early treatment and following dose changes.
onlythe smallest amount of Mirtazapine film-coated tablets should be given to the patient consistent with good patient management, in order to reduce the risk of overdose

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme): stop at once; never restart after such a reaction.

src.q: If signs and symptoms suggestive of these reactions appear, Mirtazapine should be withdrawn immediately.

items.t: Hyponatraemia (SIADH), very rare: caution in elderly or with medicines that cause hyponatraemia. Serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs: caution and closer monitoring; stop if it occurs.

src.q: Caution should be exercised in patients at risk, such as elderly patients or patients concomitantly treated with medications known to cause hyponatraemia.
Treatment with mirtazapine should be discontinued if such events occur and supportive symptomatic treatment initiated.

items.t: Akathisia usually in first weeks (increasing the dose may be harmful). Withdrawal symptoms after abrupt stop. Jaundice: stop treatment. Lactose: not for hereditary galactose intolerance.

src.q: In patients who develop these symptoms, increasing the dose may be detrimental.
Treatment should be discontinued if jaundice occurs.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Contraindicated: MAO inhibitors (and within 2 weeks).

src.q: Mirtazapine should not be administered concomitantly with MAO inhibitors or within two weeks after discontinuation of MAO inhibitor therapy.

items.t: Serotonergic drugs (L-tryptophan, triptans, tramadol, linezolid, methylene blue, SSRIs, venlafaxine, lithium, St John's wort): serotonin syndrome risk; caution and closer clinical monitoring.

src.q: co-administration with other serotonergic active substances (L-tryptophan, triptans, tramadol, linezolid, methylene blue, SSRIs, venlafaxine, lithium and St. John's Wort - Hypericum perforatum - preparations)
Caution should be advised and a closer clinical monitoring is required when these active substances are combined with mirtazapine.

items.t: Benzodiazepines and other sedatives (most antipsychotics, H1 antihistamines, opioids): more sedation, caution. Alcohol: avoid.

src.q: Mirtazapine may increase the sedating properties of benzodiazepines and other sedatives (notably most antipsychotics, antihistamine H1 antagonists, opioids).
Patients should therefore be advised to avoid alcoholic beverages while taking mirtazapine.

items.t: Warfarin: small rise in INR at 30 mg; monitor INR.

src.q: it is advisable to monitor the INR in case of concomitant treatment of warfarin with mirtazapine

items.t: QT-prolonging drugs (some antipsychotics and antibiotics): higher risk of QT prolongation/torsade de pointes.

src.q: The risk of QT prolongation and/or ventricular arrhythmias (e.g. Torsades de Pointes) may be increased with concomitant use of medicines which prolong the QTc interval

items.t: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin (inducers): mirtazapine levels fall 45% to 60%; dose may need increasing. Ketoconazole, cimetidine and other potent CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels; dose may need decreasing.

src.q: Carbamazepine and phenytoin, CYP3A4 inducers, increased mirtazapine clearance about twofold
Co-administration of the potent CYP3A4 inhibitor ketoconazole increased the peak plasma levels and the AUC of mirtazapine by approximately 40 % and 50 % respectively.

items.t: No relevant pharmacokinetic interaction with paroxetine, amitriptyline, risperidone or lithium.

src.q: Interaction studies did not indicate any relevant pharmacokinetic effects on concurrent treatment of mirtazapine with paroxetine, amitriptyline, risperidone or lithium.

items.t: Moderate to severe renal impairment (CrCl <40 ml/min): clearance may be reduced (about 30% at CrCl <40, 50% at CrCl ≤10 ml/min); take this into account when prescribing. Mild impairment (CrCl <80 ml/min): no significant difference.

src.q: The clearance of mirtazapine may be decreased in patients with moderate to severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <40 ml/min). This should be taken into account when prescribing Mirtazapine to this category of patients
No significant differences were found in patients with mild renal impairment (creatinine clearance <80 ml/min) as compared to the control group.

items.t: Clearance may be reduced (about 35% in mild to moderate impairment); take into account when prescribing, particularly in severe impairment (not studied).

src.q: This should be taken into account when prescribing Mirtazapine to this category of patients, particularly with severe hepatic impairment, as patients with severe hepatic impairment have not been investigated
the clearance of mirtazapine was approximately 35 % decreased in mild to moderate hepatically impaired patients

items.t: SmPC: limited data do not suggest a raised malformation risk. Possible risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn cannot be ruled out. Use with caution; if used until or near birth, monitor the newborn.

src.q: Limited data of the use of mirtazapine in pregnant women do not indicate an increased risk for congenital malformations.
Caution should be exercised when prescribing to pregnant women.
If Mirtazapine is used until, or shortly before birth, postnatal monitoring of the newborn is recommended to account for possible discontinuation effects.

items.t: BUMPS: can be used if recommended by a GP or specialist; no evidence of harm to development or of miscarriage/stillbirth. Later pregnancy use: hospital delivery usually advised (neonatal withdrawal; rarely PPHN with similar drugs).

src.q: Mirtazapine can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a GP or specialist.
There is no evidence that mirtazapine affects the baby's development or increases the chance of miscarriage or stillbirth.
If you take mirtazapine in later pregnancy, you will usually be advised to have a hospital delivery.

items.t: SmPC: very small amounts in milk; decide on breastfeeding versus therapy, weighing benefits.

src.q: Animal studies and limited human data have shown excretion of mirtazapine in breast milk only in very small amounts.
A decision on whether to continue/discontinue breast-feeding or to continue/discontinue therapy with Mirtazapine should be made

items.t: SPS: can be used with caution, but SSRIs or TCAs are preferred. Monitor the infant for irritability, drowsiness, GI symptoms, feeding changes and weight gain. No need to switch if used successfully in pregnancy (term, healthy infant).

src.q: Mirtazapine can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but SSRIs or TCAs are preferred.
Monitor infants for irritability, drowsiness, gastrointestinal symptoms, changes in feeding or not waking to feed, and appropriate weight gain.
there is no need to switch to a preferred choice in breastfeeding, as long as the infant has been born full term and healthy

items.t: Fertility: no effect in animal studies. Priapism reported (frequency not known).

src.q: Non-clinical reproductive toxicity studies in animals did not show any effect on fertility.
Reproductive system and breast disorders Priapism

items.t: Most common (over 5% in trials): somnolence, sedation, dry mouth, weight gain, increased appetite, dizziness, fatigue. Lowering the dose usually does not reduce sleepiness.

src.q: are somnolence, sedation, dry mouth, weight increased, increase in appetite, dizziness and fatigue
dose reduction generally does not lead to less somnolence/sedation but can jeopardize antidepressant efficacy

items.t: Also reported: headache, abnormal dreams, confusion, anxiety, insomnia, tremor, orthostatic hypotension, nausea, constipation, peripheral oedema, joint and muscle pain.

src.q: Vascular disorders Orthostatic hypotension Hypotension2 Gastrointestinal disorders Dry mouth Nausea3

items.t: Withdrawal symptoms after abrupt stopping (dizziness, agitation, anxiety, headache, nausea), mostly mild.

src.q: Among the various reported withdrawal symptoms, dizziness, agitation, anxiety, headache and nausea are the most frequently reported.

items.t: Agranulocytosis/bone marrow depression (rarely fatal): if fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers or other infection signs, stop and check blood count.

src.q: The physician should be alert for symptoms like fever, sore throat, stomatitis or other signs of infection; when such symptoms occur, treatment should be stopped and blood counts taken.

items.t: Severe skin reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS): stop immediately; never restart.

src.q: If the patient has developed one of these reactions with the use of Mirtazapine, treatment with Mirtazapine must not be restarted in this patient at any time.

items.t: Serotonin syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, myoclonus, confusion): stop and give supportive care. Seizures, jaundice, mania: stop.

src.q: Treatment with mirtazapine should be discontinued if such events occur and supportive symptomatic treatment initiated.
Treatment should be discontinued if jaundice occurs.

items.t: New or worse suicidal thoughts: seek urgent medical attention (MHRA 2026).

items.t: Once daily, preferably as a single night-time dose before bed; or two divided doses with the higher dose at night. Swallow with fluid, without chewing.

src.q: It should be taken preferably as a single night-time dose before going to bed.
The tablets should be taken orally, with fluid, and swallowed without chewing.

items.t: May impair concentration and alertness, especially at first: do not drive or use machines when affected. Avoid alcohol.

src.q: Mirtazapine may impair concentration and alertness (particularly in the initial phase of treatment).

items.t: Report fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers promptly. Seek urgent help for new or worse suicidal thoughts (NHS 111, crisis team, Samaritans 116 123). Do not stop suddenly.
